items.t: Greenwoods Asset Management's US stock holdings rise 35% in Q3, TSMC stake surges nearly twelvefold to become third-largest holding
sum: Prominent private fund manager Greenwoods Asset Management Hong Kong Ltd. filed its 13F with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) ahead of the quarterly deadline, disclosing its US stock holdings as of September 30, 2026. The filing shows total disclosed holdings of about $2.95 billion at the end of the third quarter, up about 35% from roughly $2.186 billion at the end of the second quarter. During the reporting period, Greenwoods opened three new positions, added to six, trimmed three and fully exited three, ending with 21 stocks in the portfolio. The top ten holdings accounted for 95.24% of the total.
By direction of adjustment, the semiconductor supply chain was the area of heaviest buying this quarter, while positioning in China concept stocks diverged markedly.

The most notable move of the quarter was the increase in TSMC (TSM). Greenwoods bought about 892,200 TSMC shares, lifting its stake to about 11.74 times the level at the end of the second quarter, with a period-end market value of nearly $445 million. TSMC also jumped from tenth at the end of the second quarter to third in the list of top holdings, the largest ranking gain of any position.

Other semiconductor names were also increased. Greenwoods added 1.3241 million Intel (INTC) shares, an increase of 48.13%, for a period-end market value of about $490 million, keeping it firmly in second place among top holdings. Its ASML (ASML) stake rose 158.53% to 18,300 shares.

Among new positions, Greenwoods bought 304,200 Meta (META) shares, worth about $221 million at quarter-end, entering directly as its sixth-largest holding. It also bought 118,000 Nvidia (NVDA) shares, worth about $27.04 million, and 47,300 Alibaba US shares (BABA), worth about $5.08 million.

Notably, all three were re-established after being fully exited in the second quarter. Greenwoods had sold 703,000 Alibaba shares, 540,000 Meta shares and 760,000 Nvidia shares in the second quarter. The third-quarter rebuild means its US portfolio has once again added core AI supply chain names and the leading China concept e-commerce stock.

Nvidia's shares slide after-hours as tech giant probes CEO Jensen Huang
sum: Probe follows report of Huang's relationship with Chinese businesswoman who allegedly passed information to Beijing

Nvidia shares fell in out-of-hours trading on Monday after an internal imvestigation into whether CEO Jensen Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort put his future at the AI chipmaker under scrutiny.

The internal probe followed a media report that Huang had a close relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who allegedly passed information to Beijing. Huang told Nvidia's employees that he had been unfaithful to his wife, without disclosing details of the relationship.

The investigation, announced on Sunday, has put a spotlight on Huang's future given Nvidia's status as the world's most valuable chipmaker and the CEO's role as the most prolific salesman of the AI boom.

The fallout extended to South Korea, where Madison Huang, Huang's daughter and an Nvidia executive, cancelled a planned visit to Seoul for an Nvidia conference that was set to begin on Monday, according to companies she had been scheduled to meet.

Perpetual futures trading on the Hyperliquid exchange and after-hours share trading on the Blue Ocean system showed Nvidia prices at around $178.60 a share, down more than 4% from Friday's Nasdaq closing price of $186.64.

"The market's probably telling you now this does no favours to the stock whatsoever in a time when there's a lot of conjecture as to the build out of data centres," said Chris Weston, head of research at brokerage Pepperstone in Melbourne.

sum: The chipmaker's early-stage memory plans point to a long-term bet, not a quick fix for the AI-driven shortage

TSMC has reportedly begun internal planning to manufacture advanced 3D DRAM memory chips at the request of Nvidia, one of its biggest customers. For a company that has historically stayed out of the memory business, that is a notable change of direction.
The catch: anyone hoping this ends the current memory crunch soon may need to wait. The effort is still in its early stages, with no firm capital commitments and no production timeline attached.
The reports surfaced on November 6, 2026. They describe TSMC exploring how it might produce 3D DRAM, a type of memory that builds upward rather than spreading out across a flat surface.
The project is reportedly being led by Hsu Kuo-chin, TSMC’s vice president of Advanced Packaging. His team is said to be weighing several paths forward.
Those options reportedly include building new fabrication facilities or adapting existing ones. Neither choice has been locked in.
The backdrop is a severe memory shortage driven by AI demand. That shortage is expected to weigh on both supply and pricing well into 2028.

sum: Taiwan stocks opened on Friday (the 6th) to devastating selling pressure. The Taiwan Weighted Index gapped open at 38,915.76 points before plunging in a straight line, touching an intraday low of 37,837.05 points—a collapse of 3,737.67 points, or nearly 9%—setting a record for the largest single-day intraday point drop in history. Market heavyweight Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (2330.TW) opened straight to its limit-down price of NT$2,020, a single-day plunge of NT$220, instantly wiping out roughly NT$5.7 trillion (approximately $172.8 billion) in market value and marking the largest intraday point drop on record. The number of limit-down stocks on the main board at one point exceeded 240, with electronics heavyweights and high-priced "thousand-dollar" stocks collapsing across the board as panic rapidly intensified.

The epicenter of this historic crash was the U.S. stock market. After the U.S. Midterm Elections handed Democrats control of both the Senate and the House, investors grew worried about tighter future regulation of artificial intelligence (AI) and possible restrictions on data center construction. Combined with the massive capital expenditures of large technology companies, the market began reassessing the growth prospects of AI infrastructure investment. All four major U.S. indices tumbled on the 5th: the Dow Jones Industrial Average plunged 1,833.06 points, or 3.44%, to close at 51,523.06; the S&P 500 fell 334.89 points, or 4.36%, to 7,353.73; and the Nasdaq Composite plummeted 1,421.51 points, or 5.52%, to 24,315.00—its largest single-day decline in 19 months—and has fallen more than 10% from its October record high, officially entering correction territory.

The semiconductor sector bore the brunt of the selloff. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged 1,257.52 points, or 12.25%, to close at 9,011.14. TSMC's ADR tumbled 10.78% to $353.10 (approximately NT$12,000). AI chip leader Nvidia fell 9.26%, AMD plunged 17.26%, Broadcom dropped 10.43%, Intel fell 10.33%, and memory stock Micron sank 17.46%. Market participants interpreted the Democrats' landslide midterm victory as a positive: investors bet that a White House and Congress checking each other would benefit corporate operations. Intel stock falls as TSMC eyes Elon Musk's Terafab venture
sum: Intel stock fell more than 4% in premarket trading on Monday after Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk confirmed that Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. could take part in his Terafab chip manufacturing venture in Texas — a project Intel had been first to support.

TSMC stock rose about 3% in Taiwan and was up 1% in premarket U.S. trading. The development rattled some Intel investors, who see TSMC's possible involvement as a competitive threat, given that Intel had been the earliest backer of Terafab when it pledged its support in April, according to MarketWatch.

Terafab is a joint venture between SpaceX and Tesla to manufacture chips for both companies at a site in Grimes County, Texas. Tesla and SpaceX announced the project with an initial investment of $16.8 billion and a planned workforce of at least 3,000 people. SpaceX said the chips produced there will be used in Tesla's Optimus robots and Cybercabs, as well as in space-based data centers the company is developing. Total spending across all phases could reach as much as $119 billion, the company has said.
Intel had acknowledged a role in the project but has not offered details about what that involvement entails.

TSMC's potential entry into Terafab comes as the Taiwanese chipmaker has been weighing a broader expansion of its U.S. footprint. sum: Continuing my series of "bull vs. bear" articles looking at the bull and bear theses of popular stocks, we come to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM +6.33%). The stock has been a strong performer, up around 140% over the past year and 30% year to date, as of this writing.
Let's dive into why the stock could keep hitting all-time highs, and why investors may want to take some profits.

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, or TSMC for short, is the world's leading chip manufacturer. Today, most semiconductor companies that design logic chips outsource their manufacturing to third-party foundries, like TSMC. Notably, this is much different than the memory market, where most manufacturing is done in-house.

There are a few reasons why most companies outsource their logic chip manufacturing to third parties. First, chipmaking is a capital-intensive business that involves building fabs and using very expensive extreme ultraviolet lithography (EUV) machines. By outsourcing manufacturing, chipmakers can avoid these high up-front costs. Second, semiconductor manufacturing is a scale business. Fabs (chip manufacturing facilities) need to be running near full capacity to be profitable, and that is easier with multiple customers compared to a company that is vertically integrated. And most importantly, chip manufacturing is a complex task that involves a completely different type of technological expertise that few companies have.

Foundries need to consistently shrink chip density for chips to continue to advance. At the same time, they need to maintain high yields. This means that most of the chips on a wafer need to be defect-free. This is what has set TSMC apart. While competitors have pushed down node sizes (chip density), they have run into problems maintaining adequate yields. Meanwhile, TSMC has also become the leader in advanced packaging (integrating chips and memory components into a single unit), further cementing its technological lead.

This has all led TSMC to become a virtual monopoly in the manufacturing of advanced logic chips at scale. As a result, the company has become one of the most important parts of the semiconductor value chain and a vital partner to chip designers, who must work closely with TSMC on their development roadmaps.

items.t: TSMC's Paradox: A Stock Correction That Wall Street Reads as a Bullish Signal
sum: There is an odd tension at the heart of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. right now. The company's biggest problem is that it cannot make chips fast enough to satisfy demand — and yet its share price keeps sliding. Investors have spent the past month selling a stock whose order books are, by all accounts, overflowing.

The equity trades at €347.00, roughly 17.5 percent below its early-July record high. On a 30-day basis, the decline measures 12.15 percent. Those figures would typically invite questions about whether the artificial-intelligence trade is losing steam. But the people closest to the company's operations are asking a different question entirely: not whether TSMC can find buyers, but whether it can physically produce enough silicon to keep them happy.

The constraint has shifted away from conventional chip manufacturing. It now sits squarely in advanced packaging — specifically CoWoS, the technology that makes high-end AI accelerators functional in the first place. Chief executive C.C. Wei has been candid about the squeeze in recent months, and the packaging lines are booked solid through year-end. So tight is the capacity that it is now throttling growth for TSMC's own customers.

That is an unusual position for a supplier to occupy. When your most pressing operational headache is keeping pace with your own demand, the structural story tends to outweigh short-term chart noise. It also helps explain why analysts have remained notably calm through the correction, despite a 49.09 percent annualized volatility reading that suggests calmer waters are not imminent.

The company is beginning to monetize that leverage. Strategic price adjustments across both mature and leading-edge foundry nodes are planned for early 2027 — a move less about opportunistic margin-grabbing than about recovering the enormous costs of a geographically dispersed production network. The expansion into Europe is central to that calculus: the Dresden joint venture has entered its main construction phase, with equipment installation slated for the second half of 2026. The facility represents both a step toward European chip sovereignty and, for TSMC, an insurance policy against the regional dependencies that periodically spook global markets.
